paras: The killing of a Black man in Humphreys County, Tennessee, took place shortly before Nashville dispatches of August 22-23, 1885, reported it, when a crowd that meant to beat him shot him as he tried to escape. His body was found the next morning near his cabin, and no one was arrested. The killing reached the press only as background to a Nashville dispatch on the whipping of Black residents by disguised men, which white and Black papers ran under 'Ku-Klux' headlines.

According to a Nashville dispatch of August 23, 'a more or less bitter feeling' had existed for months between certain white and Black residents of Humphreys County. The dispatch gave no cause for the hostility and named no accusation against the man who was killed.

At an unstated date before August 22, a crowd set out to beat a Black man, whose name the papers did not give. He tried to escape and was shot, and the next morning his body was found near his cabin. The dispatch called this 'the crime' and said that all efforts to find the perpetrators were futile.

Other Black residents were then taken out and 'brutally lashed', again without arrests. On a Friday shortly before the dispatches, seven disguised men drew revolvers on Samuel Low in the Duck River bottom, dragged him from his bed, and gave him more than one hundred blows with ironwood switches in the woods. The same party had already seized West Regan, who was given twenty blows and ordered to leave the county, which he did at once. A note on the door of John Gorin, a Black schoolteacher, warned him to leave or 'suffer the consequences', and he departed immediately.

No arrests were reported for the killing or the whippings, and no report of an inquest appears in the coverage. The Nashville dispatch said that 'the best citizens' of the county condemned the outrages and would likely ask the governor to offer a reward; no later report of a reward was found.

The story reached the white press as a Nashville wire item: the New York Sun printed a short version on August 23 under 'Kn-Klux Outrages in Tennessee', and the St. Paul Daily Globe carried the fuller text the next day under 'Whipping Negroes'. The Hickman Courier in Kentucky reprinted it on August 28 as 'A Race War in Tennessee', while the Delaware Daily Republican's news summary kept only the whippings and dropped the killing. In every white version the shooting took a sentence or two, overshadowed by the details of Low's beating.

The Cleveland Gazette, a Black weekly, reprinted the fuller dispatch on August 29, credited only 'Ex.'. Its headline, 'Ku-Klux Outrages', was followed by a deck of its own, 'Peaceable Negroes Brutally Beaten and Forced to Leave Their Homes in Tennessee', which stressed the victims' innocence and their expulsion. No Black paper added its own reporting or named the man who was killed.

reader.title: Killing of a Black man in Humphreys County, Tennessee (1885)
bases: A crowd that meant to beat a Black man shot him dead as he fled, and nobody was punished; the dispatch reports this killing together with whippings and warnings of other Black residents by disguised men (A1, A2, A5).

The man was shot dead by a 'crowd' that had no lawful authority and that the dispatch says committed 'the crime' (A2, A5). The size of the crowd is not given, and no accusation is stated beyond months of 'bitter feeling' between white and Black residents and the parallel Ku-Klux-style whippings (A1, A2).
Every version comes from Nashville dispatches of Aug. 22-23 (A1, A2), reprinted elsewhere (A4, A5); no local, inquest, or independent report of the killing was found, and the dead man is never named.

accounts.label: Nashville dispatch, Aug. 22
accounts.gist: A brief item: after the whippings, it adds that a Black man who 'recently attempted to escape a beating was shot and killed' and that no arrests had been made.

accounts.label: Nashville dispatch, Aug. 23
accounts.gist: A fuller version placing the killing within months of bitter feeling between white and Black residents: the man fled a crowd intent on beating him, was shot, and was found dead near his cabin the next morning; the perpetrators were not found.

framing.detail: The Sun headed the dispatch 'Kn-Klux Outrages in Tennessee', the Globe 'Whipping Negroes', and the Hickman Courier 'A Race War in Tennessee'; the text calls the killing 'the crime' and the whippings 'outrages'.
The Daily Republican's news summary reported only the whippings, omitting the killing.
The Cleveland Gazette reprinted the dispatch under 'Ku-Klux Outrages' with a deck calling the victims 'Peaceable Negroes Brutally Beaten and Forced to Leave Their Homes'.
